    <title>[8] Magnetic anisotropy, first-order metamagnetic transitions, and weak antilocalization in the candidate topological semimetal Tb2Zn17</title>
    <link>http://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/ytfq-5c74</link>
    <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> V. Kanchana, Z. Hossain</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Rajesh Swami, Papul Sahu, Sonali S Pradhan, V. Kanchana, Z. Hossain</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study of a magnetic topological semimetal, well-aligned with interest in topological materials.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#transport</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#semimetal</span></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Tb 2 Zn 17 crystallizes in the rhombohedral Th 2 Zn 17 -type structure (space group R 3 ¯ m ), a structure type known to accommodate atomic disorder. This compound shows multiple first-order field-induced metamagnetic transitions, strong magnetic anisotropy, crystal electric field effects, and possible spin canting within its antiferromagnetic state. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Magnon binding in a quantum Hall ferromagnet with a periodic electric field</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18779</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Manas Kaushik Das</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Interesting theory of magnons in quantum Hall ferromagnets.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#quantum-hall</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnon</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#ferromagnet</span></p><p><img src='data:image/png;base64,' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> A spin wave in a filling-one quantum Hall ferromagnet is neutral but carries an electric dipole perpendicular to its momentum. A spatially periodic electrostatic potential therefore creates parallel channels for spin waves. We use this established mechanism to calculate how confinement changes the exchange binding of magnons travelling in the same direction. Narrower channels increase the overlap of their transverse wavefunctions and strengthen the effective attraction. In an isolated harmonic channel, the energy required to remove one magnon from a cluster of $N$ is $\pi(k_*\ell)^4N(N-1)/4$ times the transverse level spacing to leading order, where $k_*$ is the mean wave number along the channel and $\ell$ is the magnetic length. We predict the frequency and momentum dependence of the spectral line for adding a second magnon to one already present, both in an isolated channel and in a coupled array. Tunnelling in a wide array can make the binding energy exponentially small, while a strip narrower than the transverse pair size recovers one-dimensional binding at sufficiently weak attraction. We also find that a moving potential can carry a single wave packet with less spreading than free propagation when its initial group velocity matches the potential's speed.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Lower Bound of Thermal Conductivity in Graphene</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18795</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Yahui Xue, Baowen Li</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Yan Gao, Yafei Ding, Hongbin Xu, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study of transport in graphene and phonon physics.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#graphene</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#phonon</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#transport</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/static/browse/0.3.4/images/arxiv-logo-fb.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> The intrinsic thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) of graphene remains highly controversial because of physical and metrological complexities. Although the thermal bridge method enables reliable measurements, sample fabrication remains challenging. Here, we develop a highly efficient patterning and transfer technique to systematically fabricate and characterize suspended bilayer graphene (BLG) thermal bridges with lengths of 1-30 $\mu$m. Suspended BLG with unavoidable polymer residues exhibits length-independent thermal conductivity of approximately 570 W/(m K) at room temperature, remaining nearly constant from 250 to 350 K and robust to rigorous surface cleaning and amorphous silicon nitride substrates. Homogeneous non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (HNEMD) simulations show that amorphous carbon coverage of only approximately 0.01 monolayer is sufficient to suppress out-of-plane flexural acoustic (ZA) phonons. These findings challenge the prevailing view that rigid substrates suppress ZA phonons more strongly than surface contamination and identify a robust lower bound of $\kappa$ governed by amorphous surface scattering. This lower bound reflects heat conduction in graphene under realistic device conditions and provides a reference for fundamental phonon transport studies and the integration of graphene into thermal management applications in electronic devices and chips.</p></description>

Here, we develop a highly efficient patterning and transfer technique to systematically fabricate and characterize suspended bilayer graphene (BLG) thermal bridges with lengths of 1-30 $\mu$m. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[9] Gapless Nature of Spin Liquid in the S=1/2 Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet with Neural-Network Quantum States</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18840</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Federico Becca, Luciano Loris Viteritti</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Andreas Raikos, Alessandro Sinibaldi, Riccardo Rende, Giuseppe Carleo, Federico Becca, Luciano Loris Viteritti</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 9/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> High-profile computational study on kagome magnets, highly relevant to kagome physics.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#kagome</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spin-liquid</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#quantum-magnet</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.18840v1/ssf_L16.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Whether the spin-$1/2$ kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet hosts a gapped $\mathbb{Z}_2$ or a gapless $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid remains a central open question in frustrated magnetism. Here, we address this question by directly computing the triplet gap with a neural-network quantum state that does not presuppose any specific spin-liquid structure. Applying a time-reversal symmetric transformer-based ansatz to clusters of up to $768$ sites, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies on two-dimensional lattices with periodic boundary conditions and estimate an energy per site of $-0.43873(12)$ in the thermodynamic limit. Finite-size scaling of the magnetic order parameter and triplet excitation gap shows that both extrapolate to zero in the thermodynamic limit. Together, these results provide independent and direct evidence of a gapless spin-liquid ground state, consistent with the $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid. More broadly, they demonstrate that neural-network quantum states can resolve ground-state properties of frustrated quantum magnets that remain challenging for conventional numerical methods.</p></description>

While magnetic proximity effects can lift valley degeneracy, static interfaces lack the dynamic control needed for devices. Here, we demonstrate on-demand optical switching of valley symmetry breaking in a WSe2/CrPS4 heterostructure by exploiting light-tunable magnetic order. Using polarization- and time-resolved photoluminescence, we show that excitation below the ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) gap preserves an out-of-plane N\'eel vector in CrPS4, generating a net out-of-plane spin at the interface and enabling spin-polarized charge transfer. Excitation above the LMCT gap extinguishes the polarization gap, indicating a rotation of the N\'eel vector to in-plane.       <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Satoshi Okamoto, Tom Berlijn</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Do Hoon Kiem, Satoshi Okamoto, Tom Berlijn</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Electronic structure and DFT study of Kitaev candidates.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#electronic-structure</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spin-liquid</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#DFT</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.18920v1/Figure1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> RuP$_3$SiO$_{11}$ has recently been identified as a Kitaev spin liquid candidate via neutron scattering. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19039</link>

This work opens an avenue toward compact, monolithic transverse thermopiles capable of volt-scale generation free from interfacial parasitic dissipation.</p></description>

Many theoretical and phenomenological analyses assume that the complex behaviour observed in such `quantum materials' originates either from quasi-particles dressed with an anomalous electron self-energy or from collective excitations associated with hydrodynamic flow. Despite their distinctly different starting points, the underlying assumption is that dissipation of electrical current arises from the relaxation of the total momentum of charge carriers. The distinction between classical and quantum metals becomes transparent when experimental data is analysed in terms of the current-current correlation function instead of the optical conductivity. When applied to the cuprate superconductors, such analysis uncovers that the strange metal response is present at all doping levels, and that a second, classical component develops above optimal doping. This simple, but powerful, approach further highlights essential features associated with superconductivity, (pseudo-)gaps, provides fresh insight in the properties of metals, and identifies key areas where progress in our theoretical understanding is needed.</p></description>

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19425</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Shimpei Nakamura, Motoaki Bamba</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Kazuyuki Kuroyama, Shimpei Nakamura, Motoaki Bamba</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Non-local collective dynamics in 2D electron systems relevant to ARPES/spectroscopy backgrounds.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2D-electron-gas</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetoplasmons</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/static/browse/0.3.4/images/arxiv-logo-fb.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Finite-wave-vector electromagnetic fields provide a route to accessing nonlocal collective dynamics in two-dimensional electron systems. Here, we theoretically investigate the magnetoplasmon response of a two-dimensional electron system subjected to a spatially nonuniform electromagnetic field in a perpendicular magnetic field. By combining Maxwell's equations with the Kubo formula, we derive the nonlocal magnetoconductivity tensor and obtain the self-consistent dispersion relation for collective modes. We show that a finite in-plane wave vector enables higher-order cyclotron transitions, allowing higher harmonics of the cyclotron resonance to contribute to the nonlocal conductivity. These harmonics hybridize with the magnetoplasmon mode, producing avoided crossings in the collective-mode spectrum characteristic of Bernstein modes. To quantify this hybridization, we establish a correspondence between the Maxwell-Kubo dispersion relation and a Hopfield-type Hamiltonian and derive an analytical expression for the effective coupling strength between the magnetoplasmon and the n-th cyclotron-resonance harmonic. Our analysis reveals that the normalized coupling strength exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on the in-plane wavelength, reaching a maximum that becomes nearly independent of electron density in the high-density regime. These results establish a quantitative connection between nonlocal magnetoconductivity, Bernstein-mode physics, and effective collective-mode coupling, providing design guidelines for realizing ultrastrong coupling in terahertz magnetoplasmonic systems.</p></description>

Here, we propose a magnonic field-effect device (akin to a transistor) based on a ferroelectric antiferromagnet BiFeO3 in which a gate electric field reconfigures domain boundaries to amplify/modulate magnon transport. These boundaries switch the nonlocal inverse-spin-Hall response between low- and high-signal states, with a pronounced dependence on the direction of magnon propagation. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Ferroelectric control of the K-- valley landscape in R-stacked bilayer WSe2</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19705</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Tomoaki Kameda, Kazuhito Tsukagoshi</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Katsunori Wakabayashi, Souren Adhikary, Tomoaki Kameda, Kazuhito Tsukagoshi</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Direct experimental relevance to moire/2D van der Waals materials and valley physics.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#WSe2</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2Dmaterials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#bandstructure</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.19705v1/figure1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> In bilayer WSe2 the valence-band maxima at K and {\Gamma} lie within a few thermal energies of one another, and gating redistributes holes between a light and a heavy valley of different mobilities on a landscape that stays fixed. We show that rhombohedral (R) stacking moves the landscape itself. The three-fold symmetry of R stacking forbids interlayer tunneling at K but not at {\Gamma}. The K coupling is therefore exactly zero, not merely small. A fit that leaves the coupling free returns an upper bound of 0.017 meV, three orders of magnitude under k_BT at room temperature, while the {\Gamma} coupling is 361.8 meV. The polarization creates a potential step between the layers and splits the K doublet. Each K state stays on a single layer, so the K edge shifts by half of that splitting, 41.7 meV, which any tunneling would reduce. {\Gamma} barely responds. Two consequences follow from symmetry alone, whatever the size of that shift. The two registries, carrying opposite out-of-plane ferroelectric polarizations, are exact mirror images along the displacement-field axis, and reversing the polarization reverses the displacement of the landscape. Their differential-mode transconductances are equal and opposite at zero field, where the response vanishes for an ideal nonpolar reference. The stored polarization is read out as a reversal of sign and not as a difference of current. Sweeping the field is a second route to the same parity. In the ideal symmetric limit the transconductance passes through zero at the field that cancels the polarization, 1.07 V/nm, at a single temperature. Both routes are limited by the symmetry of the device more than by the band structure. Stacking also renormalizes the landscape, so the polar one is not a translated copy of the nonpolar reference. Absolute offsets follow the exchange-correlation functional. The symmetry relations do not.</p></description>

      <title>[7] High Characteristic Voltage YBCO Josephson Junctions Written With a Focused Helium Ion Beam</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19718</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Roger K. Lake, Shane A. Cybart</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Rochelle Y. Qu, Aravind R. Sreeja, Adhilsha Parachikunnumal, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Superconducting device fabrication relevant to broader experimental condensed matter.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#superconduct</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#method</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.19718v1/Figure_1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> We report in-plane Josephson junctions written directly into YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7-\delta}$ (YBCO) thin films with a focused helium ion beam (He FIB). The characteristic voltage $I_{\mathrm{C}}R$ of these junctions, where $I_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the Josephson critical current and $R$ is the junction resistance, sets the operating frequency and the sensitivity of the circuits built from them. A single line irradiation with a dose of \SI{500}{ions/nm} across a \SI{4}{\micro\metre} wide electrode produced a junction with $I_{\mathrm{C}}R$ of 929 \si{\micro\volt} at \SI{1.6}{K}, which is `higher than the 200 to 400 \si{\micro\volt} typical of junctions fabricated previously in our laboratory. Temperature dependent resistance, current-voltage characteristics, magnetic field modulation of the critical current, and Shapiro steps under 20.5~GHz microwave irradiation show Josephson behavior with an excess current below 5 percent of the critical current. The critical current falls steeply with temperature near the junction transition and saturates at low temperature. We attribute this behavior to a barrier at the metal insulator transition, where hopping conduction through localized states is active at finite temperature and freezes out on cooling. We describe the changes in surface preparation, sample selection, beam focusing, and sample storage that accompanied the improvement, although the present data do not separate their individual contributions. Larger characteristic voltages at these dimensions are an encouraging result for rapid single flux quantum and adiabatic quantum flux parametron logic and for superconducting quantum interference devices operating at elevated temperature.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[9] Charge-Transfer Energy Governed by f-d Coulomb Interaction in Rare-Earth Systems</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19781</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Masaichiro Mizumaki, Hitoshi Sato</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Norimasa Sasabe, Shinji Watanabe, Akira Yasui, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 9/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Direct relevance to electronic structure via photoemission in strongly correlated rare-earth systems.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#photoemission</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#electronicstructure</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#correlated</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.19781v1/Fig1.jpg' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> The $f$-$d$ Coulomb interaction ($U_{\rm fd}$) plays a central role in low-energy theories describing valence fluctuations and quantum valence criticality in rare-earth systems. In contrast, core-level spectroscopies have conventionally been analyzed using the phenomenological charge-transfer energy ($\Delta$), and the relationship between these two descriptions has remained unclear. Here, we develop a spectroscopic framework demonstrating that the charge-transfer energy contains an $f$-$d$ Coulomb contribution $U_{\rm fd}n_d$ arising from the $d$-electron occupation ($n_d$), leading to the charge-transfer energy $\Delta'$. We apply this framework to the prototypical valence-transition compound YbInCu$_4$ and demonstrate, from combined analyses of core-level photoemission and $L$-edge x-ray absorption spectroscopy, that the observed spectroscopic evolution across the first-order valence transition is consistently interpreted in terms of the variation of $\Delta'$.</p></description>

In this picture, interactions between a photoexcited exciton and a Fermi sea of excess charge carriers split the exciton spectrum into a lower-energy attractive polaron branch and a higher-energy repulsive polaron branch. Due to the negligible in-plane momentum of photons, however, optical measurements probe only exciton-polarons near zero momentum, leaving their finite-momentum physics largely unexplored. Here we propose accessing this regime by measuring the absorption in the presence of an electric bias current. In effect, this displaces the electronic Fermi sea in momentum space, such that an optically active exciton-polaron at rest acquires finite momentum relative to the charge carriers. Using a diagrammatic formulation of the exciton-polaron problem, we derive exact relations between the spectral and quasiparticle properties of current-biased exciton-polarons and their finite-momentum counterparts in an equilibrium Fermi sea. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Metallic or insulating magnetic phases of transition-metal oxides in light of the Slater vs Mott controversy</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19888</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Jia-Xin Xiong, Alex Zunger</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Xiuwen Zhang, Jia-Xin Xiong, Alex Zunger</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> DFT-based discussion on Mott/Slater physics in magnetic oxides; directly relevant to correlated systems.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Mott</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Hubbard</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#DFT</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/static/browse/0.3.4/images/arxiv-logo-fb.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Magnetic d-electron oxides usually have a long-range-ordered ground state and an above-ground-state disordered para phase. The historical Slater-Mott controversy still reverberating to date pertains to understanding the origin of the insulating vs metallic nature of these two phases. Slater suggested that the insulating character evolved from the long-range order (LRO) antiferromagnetic (AFM) cell-doubling, leading to energy band repulsion and thus to forming a band gap. The reliance on LRO to explain gapping suggests that the absence of LRO in the spin-disordered para-phase would deprive the system from band repulsion, thus predicting a metallic paramagnetic (PM) phase. This, however, conflicts with numerous current observations. The alternative Mott-Peierls-Hubbard view abandons the mean-field-like band structure view emphasizing instead the local interelectronic repulsion U as a strong correlation signature of gapping both at the presence or absence of LRO. However, U is not an easily measured or calculated quantity in periodic systems, a situation often leading in practice to treating U as an adjustable parameter. The current work uses a parameter-free mean-field-like approach (Density Functional Theory, DFT), allowing energy-lowering symmetry breaking. This is done by considering local magnetic motifs as building blocks of the macroscopic AFM or PM phases. It is found that even when such motifs are isolated electronically from each other (i.e. vanishing LRO) by embedding them in quantum barriers (such as magnetic NiO6 octahedra surrounded locally by wide-gap MgO) they exhibit an intrinsic band gap. Thus, the origin of the band gaps in AFM or PM phases need not be LRO or strong correlation and can be understood within the mean-field-like band structure approach with symmetry breaking.</p></description>

It is found that even when such motifs are isolated electronically from each other (i.e. vanishing LRO) by embedding them in quantum barriers (such as magnetic NiO6 octahedra surrounded locally by wide-gap MgO) they exhibit an intrinsic band gap. Thus, the origin of the band gaps in AFM or PM phases need not be LRO or strong correlation and can be understood within the mean-field-like band structure approach with symmetry breaking.</p></content:encoded></item>

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20102</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Ingrid D. Barcelos, Felix G. G. Hernandez</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Eduardo D. Stefanato, Nicolas M. Kawahala, Ana Carolina F. de Brito, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Important study of spin-shear coupling in van der Waals magnetic materials.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#vanderWaals</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#antiferromagnet</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#THz-spectroscopy</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20102v1/fig/fig1.jpg' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Interlayer vibrations probe how magnetic van der Waals layers are stacked and coupled.       <title>[10] Surface-bulk magnetic dichotomy in intercalated transition metal dichalcogenides</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20123</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Yu He, Tianyu Zhu</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Ke Liao, Wenxin Li, Kelly Dai, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 10/10</span> <b>A_MUST_READ</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Directly impacts ARPES interpretation of magnetic TMDs; includes altermagnetism and surface/bulk sensitivity.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#ARPES</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#altermagnet</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#TMD</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetic-materials</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20123v1/fig1_combined.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Magnetically intercalated transition metal dichalcogenides are layered materials with highly tunable magnetic orders and unconventional transport properties. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Robust Antiferromagnetic Ordering above 500 K in a Family of Bilayer van der Waals Materials</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20133</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Meng Wang, Xiang Chen</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Tengda Rong, Linxin Wu, Xingke Fu, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Relevant study of high-T antiferromagnetism in 2D van der Waals materials.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#vanderWaals</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#antiferromagnet</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#neutron-scattering</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20133v1/Fig1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Stabilizing magnetic order above room temperature in layered materials is highly desirable for low-dimensional spintronics applications. Therefore, theoretical calculations predict that this robust antiferromagnetic order could persist or even strengthens at room-temperature even at the monolayer limit. Our results highlight iron-based layered oxyhalides as a promising platform for exploring beyond-room-temperature antiferromagnetism in the two-dimensional limit, holding immense potential in areas like information storage and spin-based devices.</p></description>

Devlin, Franky Bernal, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Methodological advancement in interface-specific spectroscopy relevant to heterostructures.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spectroscopy</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#heterostructure</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#method</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20198v1/Fig3_theory.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Extreme ultraviolet (XUV) second harmonic generation (SHG) combines interface selectivity with core-level element specificity but has so far been limited to linear absorption edges. Here, we measure XUVSHG from an indium tin oxide capped MoO$_3$/SiO$_2$/Si photovoltaic heterojunction for fundamental energies of 60--76\,eV, below the Si L$_{2,3}$-edge. Where linear absorption is a featureless valence background, we observe a strong, structured XUVSHG response with maxima near 70 and 76\,eV. Layer-resolved first-principles calculations reproduce both maxima and assign them to the Si/SiO$_2$ interface, the 76\,eV peak to the bridging Si monolayer and the 70\,eV peak to the near-interface substrate. Bethe--Salpeter calculations for bulk Si connect the signal to Si 2$p$ excitons at 140--160\,eV. At the Si L$_{2,3}$-edge, the calculated response is instead governed by MoO$_3$-induced asymmetry at the oxide interface. These findings establish off-edge XUV SHG as a powerful approach for selectively probing distinct buried interfaces within complex material heterostructures.</p></description>

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20235</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> R. Carrillo-Bastos, Jes\'us A. Maytorena</p><p><b>Authors:</b> M. A. Mojarro, R. Carrillo-Bastos, Jes\'us A. Maytorena</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 9/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Directly relevant theory for altermagnetism and Berry curvature optical responses.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#altermagnet</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Berry-curvature</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#theory</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20235v1/Fig1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> The momentum-dependent spin splitting and compensated magnetic order in altermagnets offer opportunities for electrical control of spin polarization. We explore the spin Edelstein effect in the frequency domain of a two-dimensional d-wave altermagnet with Rashba spin-orbit coupling. We calculate the spin-velocity susceptibility response function beyond the intraband response regime and find that the interband longitudinal and transverse Edelstein responses are governed by the Zeeman quantum metric and Zeeman Berry curvature, respectively. The density of states presents a logarithmic van Hove singularity at exactly the negative value of the energy below which four disconnected Fermi contours emerge. This defines three distinctive regions for the position of the Fermi level, through which the Edelstein susceptibility tensor displays characteristic spectral features, reflecting the topological change of the Fermi surface. The resulting spin magnetization shows a strong dependence on the driving frequency and on the orientation of the in-plane external electric field. Our results highlight new possibilities for electrical and optical control of the spin Edelstein effect in altermagnets that could find spintronic applications.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Strain-Engineering Giant Pseudo-Electric Fields in Multilayer Graphene</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20323</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Haim Beidenkopf, Nurit Avraham</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Yiwen Liu, Ambikesh Gupta, Adri\'an Ceferino, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Spectroscopic evidence of flat-band physics and topological states in graphene; high relevance to experimentalists.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#graphene</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#electronicstructure</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20323v1/Version4/Figure1_revised.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Electromagnetic scalar and vector potentials can be engineered in solids through lattice distortions, providing a versatile means of tuning electronic band structures. The pseudovector component, which generates pseudo-magnetic fields, has received much attention for its ability to realize a zero-field quantum Hall effect. However, the pseudoscalar component, giving rise to pseudo-electric fields to which many electronic systems are intrinsically susceptible, has not yet been experimentally explored. Here, we demonstrate the emergence and profound consequences of the pseudoscalar potential in a multilayer graphene system. Atomic relaxation reconstructs the system into large Bernalstacked domains separated by one-dimensional rhombohedral channels. Within this inter-dimensional system, we achieve the first direct atomic-scale imaging of distinct lattice deformations in graphene under strain. In rhombohedral channels, we observe that the tensile lattice deformation induces giant pseudo-electric fields, producing ultra-flat dispersion with divergent density of states and a large energy gap. This results in enhanced electronic correlations, leading to flat-band instabilities and striped modulation in the density of states that would otherwise require strong external displacement fields. Moreover, the gap opened by the pseudoscalar potential protects topological boundary states that persist in the absence of applied fields. Our results provide a comprehensive atomic-scale characterization of graphene elasticity and direct spectroscopic evidence for the nontrivial pseudo-electric field arising from lattice distortion. More broadly, it provides an intrinsic and tunable pathway to new quantum states</p></description>

      <title>[8] Phase diagram and lattice structure of interlayer vortices in multilayer Ising superconductors in parallel magnetic fields</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20469</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Uddalok Nag, J. K. Jain</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Subhradeep Mahata, Uddalok Nag, J. K. Jain</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Studies NbSe2; directly relevant to quasi-1D materials and superconducting properties of interest.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#NbSe2</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#superconductivity</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#STS</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20469v1/BL_Phasediag_revised_bound.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> In this work, we investigate layered $s$-wave Ising superconductors under an in-plane magnetic field using self-consistent solutions of the microscopic Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations. Comparing bilayer, four-layer, and infinite-layer systems, we determine how the phase diagram and vortex structure evolve with layer number. Compared to standard Ginzburg-Landau treatments, our approach applies over a broader parameter regime and self-consistently resolves the spatial and layer dependence of the gap amplitude without prescribing its form. We find that the field range supporting the conventional Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) phase (defined as having no interlayer vortices) is reduced with increasing layer number and is essentially absent at nonzero magnetic flux in the infinite-layer system, consistent with recent thickness-dependent experiments on multilayer 2H-NbSe$_2$. In the infinite-layer limit, the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO) phase containing interlayer vortices persists to progressively larger in-plane fields as temperature is lowered below the zero-field critical temperature, consistent with the experimentally observed low-temperature enhancement of the upper critical field. The vortex structure also evolves with interlayer hopping: in four-layer systems, for the fluxes and system sizes considered, increasing hopping reorganizes vortices from outer to inner interlayer junctions. At larger hopping, the gap distortion associated with an interior vortex extends to the surface layers, producing gap suppression comparable to that in the interior layers. Representative six-layer calculations show that interior vortices likewise produce a finite, although weaker, modulation of the surface-layer gap. These results highlight layer number and interlayer tunneling as key parameters governing the phase diagram and vortex arrangement in multilayer Ising superconductors.</p></description>

Jain</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Studies NbSe2; directly relevant to quasi-1D materials and superconducting properties of interest.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#NbSe2</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#superconductivity</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#STS</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20469v1/BL_Phasediag_revised_bound.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> In this work, we investigate layered $s$-wave Ising superconductors under an in-plane magnetic field using self-consistent solutions of the microscopic Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations. Comparing bilayer, four-layer, and infinite-layer systems, we determine how the phase diagram and vortex structure evolve with layer number. Compared to standard Ginzburg-Landau treatments, our approach applies over a broader parameter regime and self-consistently resolves the spatial and layer dependence of the gap amplitude without prescribing its form. We find that the field range supporting the conventional Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) phase (defined as having no interlayer vortices) is reduced with increasing layer number and is essentially absent at nonzero magnetic flux in the infinite-layer system, consistent with recent thickness-dependent experiments on multilayer 2H-NbSe$_2$. In the infinite-layer limit, the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO) phase containing interlayer vortices persists to progressively larger in-plane fields as temperature is lowered below the zero-field critical temperature, consistent with the experimentally observed low-temperature enhancement of the upper critical field. The vortex structure also evolves with interlayer hopping: in four-layer systems, for the fluxes and system sizes considered, increasing hopping reorganizes vortices from outer to inner interlayer junctions. At larger hopping, the gap distortion associated with an interior vortex extends to the surface layers, producing gap suppression comparable to that in the interior layers. Representative six-layer calculations show that interior vortices likewise produce a finite, although weaker, modulation of the surface-layer gap. These results highlight layer number and interlayer tunneling as key parameters governing the phase diagram and vortex arrangement in multilayer Ising superconductors.</p></content:encoded></item>

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20632</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> I. V. Solovyev</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 9/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Direct relevance to kagome magnets, orbital magnetism, and the anomalous Hall effect.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#kagome</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#anomalousHall</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20632v1/figure1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> We reveal the molecular-orbital origin of weak orbital ferromagnetism and the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) induced by noncollinear spin order in a trimerized kagome lattice. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[9] Intertwined Spin Chirality and Weyl Topology Driven Giant Hall Responses in Nd4Sb3</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20662</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Aftab Alam, P D Babu</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Anu, Subhasmita Kar, Bhagyashree Pol, Debarghya Dutta, Aftab Alam, P D Babu</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 9/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Direct relevance to magnetic Weyl semimetals, Berry curvature, and AHE experimental observables.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Weyl</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#anomalousHall</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20662v1/F1-1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Magnetic Weyl materials offer a unique platform for coupling magnetic order with real- and momentum-space topology, yet their simultaneous manifestation in a single material remains uncommon. Nd$_4$Sb$_3$ orders ferromagnetically below $T_{\mathrm{C}}\sim72$ K and undergoes spin reorientation near 42 K into a non-coplanar magnetic state. Concurrently, magnetic reconstruction profoundly reshapes the reciprocal-space topology, increasing the number of Weyl-point pairs from 42 in the collinear ferromagnetic state to 115 in the non-coplanar state. Berry-curvature calculations yield an intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity of $\sim983$ S cm$^{-1}$ at the experimentally determined carrier concentration, closely reproducing the experimental intrinsic contribution of $\sim990$ S cm$^{-1}$. These results establish Nd$_4$Sb$_3$ as a compelling platform where magnetic reconstruction intertwines real-space spin chirality with momentum-space Weyl topology.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Excitonic magnetism and competing valence bond solid instabilities in d4 ruthenium compounds</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20682</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Tomohiro Takayama, Hidenori Takagi</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Aleksandra Krajewska, Tomohiro Takayama, Hidenori Takagi</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Relevant review on strongly correlated d-electron systems and Mott physics in transition metal compounds.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Mott</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#correlated</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetism</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20682v1/excitonic_magnetism.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Spin-orbit entangled $d^4$ Mott insulators serve as a rich playground for unconventional magnetism and competing quantum electronic ground states. Intra-ionic spin-orbit coupling $\lambda_{\rm{SOC}}$ generates a non-magnetic $J_{\rm{eff}} = 0$ singlet ground state separated from an excited $J_{\rm{eff}} = 1$ triplet. The effective intra-atomic gap ${\Delta}_{\rm{eff}}$ between the ground state and lowest excited state is determined by $\lambda_{\rm{SOC}}$ and non-cubic crystal field ${\Delta}_{\rm{cf}}$. The intersite magnetic exchange $J_{\rm{ex}}$ induces dispersion of the excited $J_{\rm{eff}} = 1$ triplet. When the triplet bandwidth $W_{\rm{t}}$ overcomes ${\Delta}_{\rm{eff}}$, the system undergoes long-range magnetic ordering which is viewed as a condensation of spin-orbit excitons and called excitonic magnetism. In this review, we systematically survey representative $d^4$ ruthenium compounds across four distinct structural connectivities of Ru-ligand octahedra, from K$_2$RuCl$_6$ with isolated octahedra, corner-sharing perovskite Ca$_2$RuO$_4$, edge-sharing honeycombs, to corner-sharing pyrochlores, and map them onto a conceptual parameter axis of $W_{\rm{t}} / {\Delta}_{\rm{eff}}$. We demonstrate that $d^4$ ruthenium compounds not only represent evolution from a $J_{\rm{eff}} = 0$ Mott state to excitonic magnetism but encompass a broader competition of diverse electronic phases arising from spin-orbit coupling, exchange interactions, electron hopping, crystal field and bond covalency inhabiting similar energy scales. Near excitonic quantum critical point, where $W_{\rm{t}} \sim {\Delta}_{\rm{eff}}$, lattice geometry and chemical bonds of constituent atoms play a decisive role in selecting the electronic ground state, frequently driving valence bond solid formation that pre-empts excitonic quantum criticality.</p></description>

In this review, we systematically survey representative $d^4$ ruthenium compounds across four distinct structural connectivities of Ru-ligand octahedra, from K$_2$RuCl$_6$ with isolated octahedra, corner-sharing perovskite Ca$_2$RuO$_4$, edge-sharing honeycombs, to corner-sharing pyrochlores, and map them onto a conceptual parameter axis of $W_{\rm{t}} / {\Delta}_{\rm{eff}}$. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Unconventional Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect beyond Magnetization Scaling Driven by Pulse-Field-Induced Metamagnetism in Fe2Mo3O8</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20697</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Masashi Tokunaga, Shingo Yonezawa</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Soichiro Yamane, Sota Nakamura, Shuya Suzuki, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Magneto-optical studies of novel off-diagonal responses in magnetic phases are relevant to anomalous Hall physics.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetism</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#anomalousHall</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#opticalspectroscopy</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20697v1/fig1_2.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> First-order phase transitions often proceed through metastable states and complicated phase coexistence, yet such nonequilibrium processes are obscured in bulk measurements. The magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) probes the local off-diagonal optical response, offering access to local magnetic dynamics beyond bulk measurements. Here, we investigate the magnetic-field-induced antiferromagnetic (AFM)-ferrimagnetic (FRM) transition in the polar insulator Fe$_2$Mo$_3$O$_8$ using pulsed-field MOKE measurements extended for the first time up to 60 T and down to 1.4 K. The MOKE response exhibits unexpected and huge nonmonotonic transient behavior across the metamagnetic phase transition. The MOKE behavior does not show any scaling with the bulk magnetization, pointing to an MOKE analogue of the unconventional anomalous Hall effect. This is a new class of off-diagonal response emerging exclusively at the boundary between competing magnetic orders. At low temperatures, MOKE profiles are highly reproducible in detail, whereas at elevated temperatures they depend strongly on magnetic-field history and pulse protocol, suggesting changes in the driving mechanism of the phase transition. We infer that the excess MOKE anomaly originates from AFM-FRM phase interfaces in real space. Our results, extending MOKE into the 60 T regime, establish pulsed-field magneto-optics as a novel probe capable of uncovering transient and hidden field-induced phenomena through unconventional off-diagonal optical responses.</p></description>

Here, we investigate the magnetic-field-induced antiferromagnetic (AFM)-ferrimagnetic (FRM) transition in the polar insulator Fe$_2$Mo$_3$O$_8$ using pulsed-field MOKE measurements extended for the first time up to 60 T and down to 1.4 K. The MOKE response exhibits unexpected and huge nonmonotonic transient behavior across the metamagnetic phase transition. The MOKE behavior does not show any scaling with the bulk magnetization, pointing to an MOKE analogue of the unconventional anomalous Hall effect. This is a new class of off-diagonal response emerging exclusively at the boundary between competing magnetic orders. At low temperatures, MOKE profiles are highly reproducible in detail, whereas at elevated temperatures they depend strongly on magnetic-field history and pulse protocol, suggesting changes in the driving mechanism of the phase transition. We infer that the excess MOKE anomaly originates from AFM-FRM phase interfaces in real space. Our results, extending MOKE into the 60 T regime, establish pulsed-field magneto-optics as a novel probe capable of uncovering transient and hidden field-induced phenomena through unconventional off-diagonal optical responses.</p></content:encoded></item>

Magnetic skyrmions are prototypical examples, yet optically generating them with controlled position, type, and, in particular, chirality remains challenging.       <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Rui Chen, Dong-Hui Xu</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Zi-Ming Wang, Rui Chen, Dong-Hui Xu</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Altermagnetism in moire systems is a high-interest emerging topic in electronic structure.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#altermagnetism</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#moire</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#quasicrystals</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20952v1/Fig1.PNG' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Altermagnetism is a collinear compensated magnetic phase with zero net magnetization and momentum-dependent spin polarization. Quasicrystalline altermagnetism extends altermagnetism beyond periodic crystals, with noncrystallographic symmetries allowing high-order spin polarization patterns. Here, we propose a symmetry-based approach to realizing quasicrystalline altermagnetism by twisting collinear magnetic layers. Specifically, we demonstrate that the $30^{\circ}$-twisted honeycomb lattice bilayers form the dodecagonal quasicrystals supporting an $i$-wave altermagnetic phase. We further find that $45^{\circ}$-twisted bilayers preserving fourfold rotational symmetry support a mirror-driven $l$-wave phase with eight nodal lines. We characterize these altermagnetic patterns through plane-wave-projected spin-resolved spectral functions and spin-resolved conductances. Our work provides a systematic route to high-angular-order quasicrystalline altermagnetism through twist engineering.</p></description>

While small-angle twisted van der Waals heterostructures have been widely used to realize such physics, correlated phases are often limited by twist-angle inhomogeneity, strain, and disorder. Here, we investigate high-quality Bernal bilayer graphene placed on a patterned graphite gate, featuring a triangular array of holes, forming a new class of "gate-engineered" superlattices tunable through three independent electrostatic gates. Near the charge neutrality point, we observe insulating states characteristic of miniband formation. Temperature-dependent transport reveals activated gaps consistent with theory, and Hall measurements indicate charge-carrier inversion. Notably, the superlattice can be reconfigured electrostatically using various gate combinations, enabling flexible band-structure design without mechanical twisting. The results highlight a new route to band engineering, potentially extendable to complex periodic structures that are untenable in natural materials.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Large pseudo-orbital magnetic moment of magnons in CrI3 nanotubes</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21066</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Braga, Portugal)</p><p><b>Authors:</b> David Sanz (Universidad de Alicante, San Vicente del Raspeig, Spain), et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Magnetic excitations in 2D materials are relevant for topological and magnetic systems research.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnon</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#CrI3</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetism</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21066v1/figure1-def.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Recently discovered CrI$_3$ nanotubes are expected to host unusual radial magnetic order states, on account of the strong out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy of the two-dimensional parent material. The detection of these peculiar magnetic states is challenging, and motivates the quest for unique features that can be probed experimentally. Using linear spin-wave theory, we show that an axial magnetic field tilts the radial phase into a conical one that threads the tube with an Aharonov-Bohm flux for magnons. This flux endows magnons with a pseudo-orbital magnetic moment, reaching approximately six Bohr magnetons, three times conventional magnon spin moment, and therefore detectable through magnon spectroscopy, providing a smoking gun for the radial and conical magnetic order in CrI$_3$ nanotubes.</p></description>

    <content:encoded><p><b>Last authors:</b> Braga, Portugal)</p><p><b>Authors:</b> David Sanz (Universidad de Alicante, San Vicente del Raspeig, Spain), et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Magnetic excitations in 2D materials are relevant for topological and magnetic systems research.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnon</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#CrI3</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetism</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21066v1/figure1-def.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Recently discovered CrI$_3$ nanotubes are expected to host unusual radial magnetic order states, on account of the strong out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy of the two-dimensional parent material. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Moir\'e Excitons in a Chern Ferromagnet</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21224</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Xi Dai, Chen Hu</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Shiyu Peng, Yifan Wang, Peiyao Qin, Yixuan Liu, Xi Dai, Chen Hu</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Study of moire Chern ferromagnets links closely to topological magnetic phases of interest.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#moire</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#ferromagnet</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21224v1/fig1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Recent experiments have established excitonic optical resonances as powerful probes and control knobs of moir\'e Chern ferromagnets. However, the microscopic nature of excitons formed on such interaction-driven, time-reversal-symmetry-broken ground states remains largely unexplored. In this paper, using a Gutzwiller plus Bethe-Salpeter equation framework, we investigate twisted bilayer MoTe2 at hole filling {\nu}_h=1 and identify two near-infrared Chern-ferromagnet excitons (CFEs) selectively coupled to opposite circular polarizations. Strong electron-hole interactions markedly enhance their energy separation and drive a pronounced momentum-space reconstruction of the emergent X- state, beyond the quasiparticle-transition picture. We further find that this reconstruction enhances the interlayer electron-hole character of X-, giving rise to a giant quadratic Stark response. These findings reveal the nontrivial interplay between electron-electron correlations and electron-hole interactions underlying CFE formation, providing optical fingerprints of moir\'e Chern-ferromagnetic order and a microscopic basis for its optical control.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Failure of Mean-Field Critical Scaling and Two Distinct Dissipation Regimes in La2SmNi2O7-</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21536</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Junjie Zhang, Hai-Hu Wen</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Yongze Ye, Feiyu Li, Di Peng, Junjie Zhang, Hai-Hu Wen</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study of critical scaling and vortex dynamics in superconducting nickelates.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#material</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#superconductivity</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#experiment</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#nickelate</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21536v1/Fig_rho_T.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Recently, superconductivity with an onset transition temperature ($T_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{onset}}$) up to 96 K has been observed in the $\mathrm{La}_{2-x}\mathrm{Sm}_{1+x}\mathrm{Ni}_2\mathrm{O}_{7-\delta}$ system under pressure, providing an attractive platform for investigating superconducting mechanisms in nickelates. Here, we systematically analyzed the critical scaling and vortex dynamics for the $\mathrm{La}_2\mathrm{Sm}\mathrm{Ni}_2\mathrm{O}_{7-\delta}$ single crystal with $T_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{onset}}=92.5$ K under pressure. Within the Ullah--Dorsey framework, neither the two-dimensional nor three-dimensional scaling provides a good collapse near $T_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{MF}}$. This failure may be associated with the multiband composite order parameter of bilayer nickelates, in which pairing is mainly driven by antiferromagnetic exchange in the $d_{z^2}$ orbital, whereas the superfluid stiffness is mainly governed by the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital. The two-step decrease in the logarithmic resistivity reveals two distinct dissipative regimes. The low-temperature regime is well described by the thermally assisted flux flow (TAFF) model, whereas the high-temperature regime cannot be explained by the vortex dynamics involved with the superconducting fluctuation. The crossover between the two regimes may be associated with the orbital-dependent evolution of vortex cores. These results suggest the significant role of the composite order parameter in critical fluctuations and vortex-motion dissipation in nickelates.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[9] Non-Topological Chiral Anomaly: The Chiral Magnetoelectric Effect</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18841</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> J\'er\'emie Quevillon, Diego Saviot</p><p><b>Authors:</b> R\'emy Larue, Amaury Marchon, J\'er\'emie Quevillon, Diego Saviot</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 9/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Direct relevance to Weyl semimetals, topological physics, and proposed experimental magnetoelectric effect.; demoted from A: broad CM, not direct user/project hit</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Weylsemimetals</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#transport</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetoelectricity</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#chiralanomaly</span></p><p><img src='data:image/png;base64,' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> We derive the chiral anomaly in a thermal medium and show that, in addition to the well-established topological piece, the anomaly acquires a previously overlooked non-topological contribution, relevant for non-gauged axial symmetries. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Tunable Multi-Frequency-Band Generator and Detector of AC Signals Based on a Spin Hall Device with Two Antiferromagnetic Layers</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19004</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Volodymyr Prokopenko, Oleksandr Prokopenko</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Oleh Shtanko, Volodymyr Prokopenko, Oleksandr Prokopenko</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Theoretical study of spin Hall devices with antiferromagnetic layers, relevant to magnetic materials and spin transport.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#antiferromagnetism</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spinHalleffect</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spintronics</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#devicephysics</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magneticmaterials</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.19004v1/Fig_1.jpg' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Antiferromagnetic (AFM) spin Hall oscillators offer an electrical route to compact terahertz sources, while AFM spin Hall diodes can be used as a promising detectors of terahertz signals, however, their attainable frequency and the redout efficiency are constrained by the dynamics of a single AFM layer. We theoretically and numerically investigate a spin Hall multilayer junction Pt/AFM/Pt/AFM/Pt comprising two canted AFM layers, driven by independent drive DC currents flowing in the outer platinum (Pt) layers. Using a model based on the coupled Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert-Slonczewski equations for four AFM sublattices and a phase-dependent two-interface spin Hall magnetoresistance model, we show that the device manifests itself as a DC current-driven oscillating spin Hall magnetoresistance. When an additional DC (AC) signal current is applied to the junction, the device generates an output AC (DC) voltage. Our model predicts current-driven, locked, co- and counter-rotational states of the net magnetization at Neel-vector frequencies in the top and bottom AFM layers, respectively. These states result in a multi-frequency response of the spin Hall magnetoresistance at the sum and difference frequencies. The counter-rotation regime additionally activates the phase-sensitive mixing contribution, producing a fourth harmonic. In contrast, the co-rotation regime provides a difference-frequency channel on the order of 100 GHz, although mutual locking prevents this output from being tuned continuously toward zero. Our estimations show that the device matched to an external load can generate output AC power of 1.2 nW at the second harmonic and 0.8 pW at the fourth harmonic, and can produce a DC voltage of about 1 mV for a 6 mA input signal current.</p></description>
